chapter: Louis Jordan, Ink Spots and the union
title: Working with Charlie Gray's Ink Spots and Deek Watson
summary: He freelanced with Charlie Gray's Ink Spots and Deek Watson, noting Gray was egotistical and paid the band last, then drifts to friends in Seattle.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: For you what was the most -- you were saying the other day, like -- that the most satisfying thing
was working with your own group?
But then other opportunities would come up.
Other opportunities would come up. Just anybody that wanted me to work with them, I'd work with them. Just a gig, you know, and I'd go right on and make that money.
I figured I could make it better by just going on and working with whoever come after me to work, I'd work with them, you know?
Like Charlie Gray and the Ink Spots, his Ink Spots, not the original.
That was the same Charlie Gray, then, that was with Louis Jourdan.
Yeah. And then I worked with Deek Watson.
He was one of the original Ink Spots.
I guess he is. I don't know nothing about him right now. Don't know where he is. I know he's a funny person. He's stuck, stuck on himself, you know. But he can dress. He really can dress.
Yeah. He can dress. But he's what you call agotistic -- egotistic, or something.

Yeah. It's funny. Now, I've never been like that in my life. I don't see how a person could be like that, I mean making the money Charlie Gray was. Why would he be like that, working every day, every night?
People, you know, react differently to success.

They do, because he did. The nights he'd pay us off he'd take the singers first, pay them off, then the background, the band, you know, he'd make them be last. The ones that were helping him the most.
So he was thinking about the show biz.
Yeah. Yeah, we'd be the last ones. The only one he'd pay before me and the others, you know, would be the bass player, his singers.

We had one come back there and he went back to the Post Office, he got so mad and brought down, he went on back to the Post Office. And he was one of the singers. Monroe Powell. He was one of the singers. He was a nice looking boy, yellow, you know, and he had a lot of chicks all the time. So he married a Canadian girl. They had a child. So he finally moved to Seattle and stayed there, as far as I know of.
Yeah. You have some friends up there, right?
Who's that Italian family up there?
Oh, boy, oh, boy, oh, boy.
Raga -- oh -- what did you say?

I mean I know I've got it wrong. I was thinking of something like Ragatelli, or Rafatelli, or something. That's not exactly right. It's in the ballpark, but that's not it, you know. But they ran a club up there, right?
And he's a member of the Elks up there.
